name: Tromsø
title: Holidays in Tromsø
intro: Husky sledding, reindeer and the northern lights, high in the Arctic Circle. Here's what Tromsø is like with the family, when to go and how long to stay.
facts_note: Norway follows Europe's border rules. Check entry rules on GOV.UK before you book.
when_to_go: January to March has snow for husky sledding and dark skies for the northern lights, with daylight coming back by February. From late November to mid-January the sun doesn't rise at all. In summer the sun never sets, which is great for hiking and fjord trips.

things.name: Northern lights chase
things.blurb: Guides drive out to wherever the skies are clearest. Most tours have hot drinks and a campfire.

things.name: Husky sledding
things.blurb: Ride in a sled pulled by a team of dogs, then meet the puppies.

things.name: Reindeer and Sámi camp
things.blurb: Feed reindeer and hear stories in a lavvu tent from the Sámi people.

things.name: Fjellheisen cable car
things.blurb: Up the mountain for huge views over the island city.

things.name: Polaria
things.blurb: An Arctic aquarium with bearded seals, in a building shaped like ice floes.

things.name: Arctic Cathedral
things.blurb: A striking white church with candlelit concerts in winter.

faqs.question: Is Tromsø good for a family holiday?
faqs.answer: Yes, for a once-in-a-lifetime winter trip. Most activities suit children from around four, though check age limits on longer night tours.

faqs.question: How many nights do you need?
faqs.answer: Four or five nights gives you several chances to see the northern lights and time for a husky and a reindeer trip.

faqs.question: Do UK families need a visa?
faqs.answer: No, British passport holders can visit Norway for up to 90 days in any 180 without a visa. New European entry checks are being brought in, so check GOV.UK before you travel.

faqs.question: How cold is it?
faqs.answer: Usually around -5°C in winter, milder than you might expect thanks to the Gulf Stream. Tour companies lend thermal suits and boots.
